content.purpose: Know what you are actually talking to before you start typing at it.
content.mentalModel: Four different things get called "Linux". The kernel is the program that manages hardware, memory and processes. A distribution such as Debian is the kernel plus thousands of programs packaged together. The shell is a program that reads what you type and runs it; here that shell is Bash. The terminal is just the window the shell's text appears in. When someone says "learn Linux", they almost always mean learn the shell.

demonstration.explanation: Prints the kernel name, and nothing else. This is the kernel, not the distribution.
Everything the kernel will tell you about itself: name, host name, version, build date and architecture.
This is the distribution. Debian writes its identity into a file, and cat prints the file.

remember: The kernel manages hardware; the distribution is the kernel plus its software; the shell runs your commands; the terminal displays them
uname describes the kernel and says nothing about which distribution you are on
/etc/os-release is where a Linux system records which distribution it is

commonOptions.meaning: Print only the kernel release, useful in scripts
Print the machine architecture, such as x86_64

tasks.instruction: Ask the kernel to describe itself in full, and write what it says into a file called kernel.txt in your home directory. Use a redirect: put > kernel.txt on the end of the command.

validators.message: kernel.txt exists but does not contain the kernel's output. Check that you redirected uname and not something else.
kernel.txt contains only the kernel name. Use uname's option that prints the full kernel and machine description.

hints: One command prints information about the kernel. You saw it in the example above.
The option that prints everything is -a.
Adding > kernel.txt to the end of a command sends its output into that file instead of the screen.

tasks.instruction: Find out which Linux distribution this system is, and save the line that names it into distribution.txt in your home directory. The file must contain the word Debian.

validators.message: distribution.txt does not mention Debian. The distribution's name is recorded in a file under /etc.

hints: The kernel does not know which distribution it is running. The distribution records that itself, in a file.
You can redirect the whole file: cat /etc/os-release > distribution.txt

reviewQuestions.question: Which of these is the program that reads the commands you type and runs them?
reviewQuestions.explanation: The shell, here Bash, interprets what you type. The terminal only displays it, and the kernel only runs the resulting programs.

reviewQuestions.question: You run uname -a and see the word Linux. What have you learned about the distribution?
answers: Nothing: uname describes the kernel, not the distribution
reviewQuestions.explanation: Every distribution runs the Linux kernel, so uname cannot tell them apart. /etc/os-release can.
